question.text: An organic compound '<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></math>' on reaction with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>NH</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math> followed by heating gives compound <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></math>. Which on further strong heating gives compound <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></math> <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfenced><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mn>8</mn></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><msub><mi>NO</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mfenced></math>. Compound <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></math> on sequential reaction with ethanolic <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>KOH</mi></math>, alkyl chloride and hydrolysis with alkali gives a primary amine. The compound <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></math> is

solution.text:
The carboxylic acids on heating with ammonia give amides. A diamide on strong heating give an imide.

Gabriel Phthalimide reaction: The hydrogen of the imide is acidic which can be extracted with base. Now, the nucleophile formed undergo bimolecular nucleophilic substitution reaction with alkyl chloride. Now, the alkyl imide undergo hydrolysis to give primary amine.
